pages.title: Teradyne enhances Titan HP for AI chip reliability tests - Engineering.com
pages.text:
The production-ready system runs device workloads at target junction temperatures and records each device’s stress history.
Teradyne, Inc. announced a production-ready system that delivers enhanced burn-in capabilities on its Titan HP platform. Traditional burn-in holds devices in banks of dedicated ovens at a controlled air temperature for hours before they move on to functional test. Teradyne Titan HP instead holds each device at its target junction temperature while running a realistic device workload, so reliability stress functions are optimized and thermal controls are enabled at the per-device level. Titan HP can be used for system level test or reliability testing, optimizing capital cost investments. For reliability testing, every device carries its full stress-and-test history on a single record.
Teradyne introduces Titan HP with burn-in for advanced AI data center devices
Per-site thermal control, tuned to each device’s thermal and force zones, a.nd paired with high per-device kilowatt power delivery, lets Titan HP sustain reliability-stress conditions on parts whose power draw and heat dissipation strain a conventional oven flow. The platform’s asynchronous slot architecture loads and tests each slot independently, so a long stress run on one device does not idle the rest of the system, and individual sites can be serviced while the system continues to operate.
Test programs run on the Teradyne Atlas software platform, which lets engineers import existing programs or build new ones and port them to other Teradyne system level test systems. Teradyne’s per-device power roadmap extends to the levels future AI accelerators are expected to require, so the same platform carries customers forward as device power grows.
Burn-in has long been standard for automotive and other high-reliability silicon. AI accelerators and cloud infrastructure devices are now entering the same category, driven by the high cost of a single failed accelerator in a deployed rack. That demand is arriving as capital, floor space, and handling capacity for dedicated oven banks come under pressure in high-volume manufacturing and OSAT facilities.
Enhanced burn-in extends Teradyne’s test portfolio, which spans the AI device supply chain from wafer to data center. As AI silicon moves through wafer probe, package test, system level test, and now reliability stress testing, Teradyne covers every device at every insertion.
Teradyne Titan HP with enhanced burn-in is available now and deployed in production.

Teradyne Strengthens Pre-Shipment Testing for AI Semiconductors
U.S.-based Teradyne announced that it has enhanced reliability testing for AI semiconductor equipment.
The company aims to achieve both quality and production efficiency through per-chip temperature control and test history tracking.
A hint for work: in addition to asking "is it finished?", ask "have I verified it under the conditions in which it will be used?"
In discussions about AI, attention often turns to the semiconductors that perform calculations or the convenient services they power. Behind the scenes, U.S.-based Teradyne is a company that handles the equipment used to verify whether these semiconductors function as expected.
On October 6, 2026 (local time), the company announced that it has enhanced the burn-in functionality of its semiconductor test equipment, the "Titan HP." Burn-in is a test that verifies component reliability by applying loads such as temperature and power. [1]
The equipment itself was already announced in October 2025. [3] The news this time lies in the fact that the reliability testing capabilities of the existing equipment have been strengthened. The company explains that the enhanced version has begun shipping and is already being used on production floors. [1]
Regarding conventional methods, the company explains that the process involves managing the ambient air temperature in a dedicated oven for a certain period before proceeding to verify functionality.
With the Titan HP, the internal temperature of each chip is maintained at a target value while running processes close to actual usage. The concept is to verify the chip by combining operation and temperature to approximate the conditions during real-world use.
According to the product page, the entire system can continue to operate even while individual test sites are being serviced. The load and test history for each component are also consolidated into a single record. This is a mechanism that allows for tracking what was verified and under what conditions. [2]
What can be expected and what remains unknown
The company states that this can reduce inspection costs and floor space, as well as shorten the time to market for products. This is the expectation presented by the company. This announcement does not include specific comparative results, such as by what percentage costs were reduced or how much the failure rate improved. [1]
Furthermore, one cannot judge that the same effect will be achieved for all customers based solely on the explanation that it is "being used on production floors." The actual effect must be viewed in the context of the items being inspected and the operational conditions.
In corporate news, it is easier to understand if one separates the fact that a product has been released from the results expected thereafter. It is also important not to interpret the announcement of a new feature directly as an increase in sales or profits.
What can be gleaned from this announcement is that making quality verification easier to incorporate into daily tasks is also a form of product value. This is an interpretation based on the content of the announcement.
For example, a business tool that works with a small amount of data might produce different results during concentrated end-of-month processing. Even if a procedure manual is easy for the creator to understand, it may be difficult for someone handling it for the first time. The significance of adding the perspective of "how it is actually used" to the verification of completion applies to more than just semiconductors.

AI Chips Need Testing, and Teradyne (TER) Is Winning. Is the Valuation Too High?
Robots get the headlines at Teradyne (NASDAQ:TER). Chip testers pay the bills. In the second quarter of 2026, the company's robotics arm brought in $100 million. Its semiconductor test business brought in $1.12 billion over the same three months.
That split matters, because the stock isn't cheap. Teradyne builds the machines that check chips for defects before they ship, a step every AI processor and memory chip has to clear. It also owns Universal Robots, a maker of collaborative robot arms (cobots, built to work beside people) found on factory floors around the world. That operational momentum earns the stock a spot among the 10 High-Beta Stocks with Strong Revenue Growth. So what are investors actually paying for at 44 times expected earnings? The answer depends less on the robots than on how long the testing boom lasts.
AI Chips Need Testing, and Teradyne (TER) Is Winning. Is the Valuation Too High?
The second quarter was Teradyne's second straight record. Revenue hit $1.33 billion, up 104% from $652 million a year earlier, and beat the top of management's own guidance. Adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings per share came in at $2.47, against $0.57 a year before.
Memory was a big driver. Teradyne posted record memory revenue on continued DRAM strength and a revival in NAND final test, the last check flash chips get before shipping. The AI build-out is clearly pulling on more than just processors; a tailwind memory chipmakers like Micron are riding too.
Pricing power shows up in the margins. Gross margin came in at 59.8%, and CEO Greg Smith said rising wafer fab equipment spending sets the company up for growth in 2027 and beyond.
Robotics is small, but it's no longer just about arms. At the Automate trade show earlier this year, Teradyne Robotics showed off what it calls production-ready physical AI, robots that adapt to messy surroundings instead of repeating one motion. Its first physical AI product, the MiR1200 Pallet Jack, is already for sale.
The more telling detail was who else showed up. Partners demonstrated AI bin picking from Vention, imitation-learning tools built with Scale AI, and dual-arm robots threading copper cables into server racks, all running on Universal Robots hardware. Teradyne also taps Nvidia's GR00T model and Isaac Sim simulation software. When outside developers build on your arms, the platform starts to look like a standard, which keeps Teradyne in the conversation about robotics stocks betting on physical AI.
Has the Testing Cycle Peaked?
Here's the worry. Teradyne guided third-quarter revenue to $1.2 billion to $1.3 billion, below the record $1.33 billion it posted in the second quarter. Adjusted EPS guidance of $1.85 to $2.15 also sits under the second quarter's $2.47. Gross margin had already slipped to 59.8% from 60.9% in the first quarter.
Chip testing has always been cyclical, and a step down after a record can be the first sign of a plateau. Robotics, at $100 million a quarter, is far too small to cushion a semiconductor slowdown. Management's guidance still credits strong AI-related demand, though, and its 2027 outlook doesn't read like a company bracing for a bust. One softer quarter wouldn't break the story. Two in a row would, leaving valuation-conscious investors looking elsewhere, as Teradyne misses out on the 10 Best Affordable Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street Analysts.
At 44.29 times forward earnings, as of October 12, Teradyne trades well above the sector's 23.29. It also sits above its own five-year average of 35.27, so investors are paying up even by Teradyne's standards.
Growth is the defense. Analysts expect earnings to grow 28.17% in 2027. That's fast, but it doesn't fully explain a multiple this far above the stock's own history. The price assumes AI testing demand keeps rolling for years and that robotics eventually becomes a real earnings contributor rather than a side story. It's the same tension running through AI chip equipment stocks, where booming orders meet stretched multiples.
Short interest sits at 6.38% of the float, meaning a noticeable slice of traders is betting the rally has gone too far. Hedge funds moved the other way, with 82 holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 80 in the prior one.
The evidence says investors are paying for the testing boom, with robotics as an option on top. That boom is real, and the 2027 growth forecast gives the premium some cover. The setup suits growth investors who can stomach chip-cycle swings and believe AI test demand lasts into 2027. If the third quarter lands inside guidance and management holds its 2027 view, 44 times earnings looks defensible. A second straight sequential decline, or fading memory strength, would make it look like peak pricing.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of TER as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. A hint for work: in addition to asking "is it finished?", ask "have I verified it under the conditions in which it will be used?"
In discussions about AI, attention often turns to the semiconductors that perform calculations or the convenient services they power. Behind the scenes, U.S.-based Teradyne is a company that handles the equipment used to verify whether these semiconductors function as expected.
On October 6, 2026 (local time), the company announced that it has enhanced the burn-in functionality of its semiconductor test equipment, the "Titan HP." Burn-in is a test that verifies component reliability by applying loads such as temperature and power. [1]
The equipment itself was already announced in October 2025. [3] The news this time lies in the fact that the reliability testing capabilities of the existing equipment have been strengthened. The company explains that the enhanced version has begun shipping and is already being used on production floors. [1]
Regarding conventional methods, the company explains that the process involves managing the ambient air temperature in a dedicated oven for a certain period before proceeding to verify functionality.
With the Titan HP, the internal temperature of each chip is maintained at a target value while running processes close to actual usage. The concept is to verify the chip by combining operation and temperature to approximate the conditions during real-world use.
According to the product page, the entire system can continue to operate even while individual test sites are being serviced. The load and test history for each component are also consolidated into a single record. This is a mechanism that allows for tracking what was verified and under what conditions. [2]
What can be expected and what remains unknown
The company states that this can reduce inspection costs and floor space, as well as shorten the time to market for products. This is the expectation presented by the company. This announcement does not include specific comparative results, such as by what percentage costs were reduced or how much the failure rate improved. [1]
Furthermore, one cannot judge that the same effect will be achieved for all customers based solely on the explanation that it is "being used on production floors." The actual effect must be viewed in the context of the items being inspected and the operational conditions.
In corporate news, it is easier to understand if one separates the fact that a product has been released from the results expected thereafter. It is also important not to interpret the announcement of a new feature directly as an increase in sales or profits.
What can be gleaned from this announcement is that making quality verification easier to incorporate into daily tasks is also a form of product value. This is an interpretation based on the content of the announcement.
For example, a business tool that works with a small amount of data might produce different results during concentrated end-of-month processing. Even if a procedure manual is easy for the creator to understand, it may be difficult for someone handling it for the first time. The significance of adding the perspective of "how it is actually used" to the verification of completion applies to more than just semiconductors.

AI Chips Need Testing, and Teradyne (TER) Is Winning. Is the Valuation Too High?
Robots get the headlines at Teradyne (NASDAQ:TER). Chip testers pay the bills. In the second quarter of 2026, the company's robotics arm brought in $100 million. Its semiconductor test business brought in $1.12 billion over the same three months.
That split matters, because the stock isn't cheap. Teradyne builds the machines that check chips for defects before they ship, a step every AI processor and memory chip has to clear. It also owns Universal Robots, a maker of collaborative robot arms (cobots, built to work beside people) found on factory floors around the world. That operational momentum earns the stock a spot among the 10 High-Beta Stocks with Strong Revenue Growth. So what are investors actually paying for at 44 times expected earnings? The second quarter was Teradyne's second straight record. Revenue hit $1.33 billion, up 104% from $652 million a year earlier, and beat the top of management's own guidance. Adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings per share came in at $2.47, against $0.57 a year before.
Memory was a big driver. Teradyne posted record memory revenue on continued DRAM strength and a revival in NAND final test, the last check flash chips get before shipping. The AI build-out is clearly pulling on more than just processors; a tailwind memory chipmakers like Micron are riding too.
Pricing power shows up in the margins. Gross margin came in at 59.8%, and CEO Greg Smith said rising wafer fab equipment spending sets the company up for growth in 2027 and beyond.
Robotics is small, but it's no longer just about arms. At the Automate trade show earlier this year, Teradyne Robotics showed off what it calls production-ready physical AI, robots that adapt to messy surroundings instead of repeating one motion. Its first physical AI product, the MiR1200 Pallet Jack, is already for sale.
The more telling detail was who else showed up. Partners demonstrated AI bin picking from Vention, imitation-learning tools built with Scale AI, and dual-arm robots threading copper cables into server racks, all running on Universal Robots hardware. Teradyne also taps Nvidia's GR00T model and Isaac Sim simulation software. When outside developers build on your arms, the platform starts to look like a standard, which keeps Teradyne in the conversation about robotics stocks betting on physical AI.
Has the Testing Cycle Peaked?
Here's the worry. Teradyne guided third-quarter revenue to $1.2 billion to $1.3 billion, below the record $1.33 billion it posted in the second quarter. Adjusted EPS guidance of $1.85 to $2.15 also sits under the second quarter's $2.47. Gross margin had already slipped to 59.8% from 60.9% in the first quarter.
Chip testing has always been cyclical, and a step down after a record can be the first sign of a plateau. Robotics, at $100 million a quarter, is far too small to cushion a semiconductor slowdown. Management's guidance still credits strong AI-related demand, though, and its 2027 outlook doesn't read like a company bracing for a bust. One softer quarter wouldn't break the story. Growth is the defense. Analysts expect earnings to grow 28.17% in 2027. That's fast, but it doesn't fully explain a multiple this far above the stock's own history. The price assumes AI testing demand keeps rolling for years and that robotics eventually becomes a real earnings contributor rather than a side story. It's the same tension running through AI chip equipment stocks, where booming orders meet stretched multiples.
Short interest sits at 6.38% of the float, meaning a noticeable slice of traders is betting the rally has gone too far. Hedge funds moved the other way, with 82 holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 80 in the prior one.
The evidence says investors are paying for the testing boom, with robotics as an option on top. That boom is real, and the 2027 growth forecast gives the premium some cover. The setup suits growth investors who can stomach chip-cycle swings and believe AI test demand lasts into 2027. If the third quarter lands inside guidance and management holds its 2027 view, 44 times earnings looks defensible. A second straight sequential decline, or fading memory strength, would make it look like peak pricing.
